newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran says quake relief arriving, rescue ended.
newsitem.headline: Iran says quake relief arriving, rescue ended.

text.p: International aid to survivors of a deadly earthquake which left 50,000 people homeless in eastern Iran trickled in as Tehran said rescue work had ended and announced plans to start rebuilding quake-stricken villages.

Planes from Azerbaijan, Jordan, Kuwait, Pakistan, Turkey and Syria on Tuesday landed in Mashhad, capital of quake-hit Khorasan province, with 130 tonnes of emergency aid and food, state-run Tehran radio said on Wednesday.

Rasul Zargar, Iran's top official in charge of natural disasters relief, earlier said rescue teams on Tuesday ended their operations in 200 villages devastated by Saturday's quake which measured 7.1 on the Richter scale, the radio said.
Iran has revised downward casualty figures, saying the latest figures were 1,560 dead and 2,810 injured. An official said earlier reports of 2,400 dead and 6,000 injured were inaccurate.
Zargar said the government was assessing damage and would launch a massive reconstruction programme in early June, giving two million rials ($670) to owners of each house destroyed.
An initial estimate of the damage was 600 billion rials ($200 million), he added. Tehran has allocated 500 billion rials ($167 million) for reconstruction.
A United Nations report released in Tehran said a mission to the area confirmed the massive destruction of villages and heavy damage to power lines, roads and irrigation systems.
It said Iran was asking foreign donors for food, medicine, heaters, power generators, clothes, tents and blankets.
Relief work is led by Iran's Red Crescent assisted by army units and a powerful Shi'ite Moslem endowment run by clerics appointed by Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

In Geneva, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it had raised seven million Swiss francs ($4.6 million) towards its 12 million Swiss franc ($8.2 million) appeal issued on Monday to help quake victims.
The money was raised from four governments -- Britain, Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway -- and from 13 national Red Cross or Red Crescent societies.
Several countries made pledges or said they had sent aid, including Iran's arch-foe the United States and European Union states involved in a diplomatic row with Tehran.
($1=3,000 rials at the official exchange rate)
